prompt.context: The CEO of General Motors attended the Detroit car show recently. He was surprised to see that all the models of Volkswagens seemed to have the same steering wheel. They seemed similar in all respects — shape, size, and materials. General Motors, on the other hand, has many different steering wheels for its many cars. The CEO feels there was merit in reducing the steering wheels on GM cars to one model.
prompt.question: He wants you to find out how that can be done — specifically, whether and how GM should consolidate its steering wheel types to a single model.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any difference in material requirements across the different steering wheel types?
clarifying_info.a: There is virtually no difference in material requirements for each type of steering wheel.

clarifying_info.q: Is the same manufacturing process used for all steering wheel types?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the same injection molding manufacturing process is currently used to make the different steering wheels.

clarifying_info.q: Are there engineering differences that require different steering wheels for different car models?
clarifying_info.a: There is virtually no difference in engineering design requirements. From an engineering perspective, the same wheel could be used on all cars.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a customer or market reason for having different steering wheels?
clarifying_info.a: There is no market requirement — neither customer-driven nor company-promoted — to have different steering wheels. Steering wheels do not serve as product differentiators.

clarifying_info.q: How many car lines does GM have, and how many steering wheels does it buy?
clarifying_info.a: GM has 10 lines of cars, each with a different type of steering wheel. Each year 100,000 steering wheels are bought for each line, for a total of 1,000,000 per year.

clarifying_info.q: Who supplies the steering wheels and at what price?
clarifying_info.a: GM purchases all 10 types from the same supplier at $10 each.

The supplier gives a 5% discount for every doubling of order size. Additionally, if GM consolidates to one type and buys all wheels from one vendor, the vendor will give a 20% discount on the steering wheel.

framework: Identify the objective: cost reduction through parts consolidation
Check manufacturing feasibility: materials, process, engineering design
Check market/competitive impact: customer demand, product differentiation
Quantify financial benefit: current cost baseline vs. consolidated cost scenarios
Assess risks and implementation requirements before executing
Identify further consolidation opportunities across other car components

questions.prompt: What is GM's current annual spend on steering wheels, and what savings could be achieved through consolidation?
questions.guidance: Strong answers establish the baseline first, then model two discount scenarios separately before combining them. The candidate should recognize that consolidating 10 types into 1 means multiplying the per-type order by 10 (from 100k to 1M units), then apply the 5% per doubling rule correctly across 3 doublings, and separately evaluate the single-vendor 20% discount. A top candidate will note both discounts may stack.

math.setup: Current spend: 10 lines × 100,000 wheels/line × $10/wheel = $10,000,000/year. Consolidation to 1 type: order size goes from 100,000 to 1,000,000 — that is 10× increase, which is between 3 and 4 doublings. Strictly 3 doublings (100k→200k→400k→800k) = 3×5% = 15% discount; the 4th doubling would reach 1,600k, so for 1,000,000 units use 3 doublings = 15%. Single-vendor additional discount: 20%.
steps: Volume discount (3 doublings): 15% off → price per wheel = $8.50; spend = $8,500,000; savings = $1,500,000 (15%)
Single-vendor discount (20%): price per wheel = $8.00; spend = $8,000,000; savings = $2,000,000 (20%)
Combined (if both apply): 20% single-vendor discount applies to the consolidated order → effective price = $8.00/wheel; total spend = $8,000,000
Sample solution states 'at least 32%' savings, suggesting both discounts compound: $10 × (1-0.15) × (1-0.20) = $10 × 0.85 × 0.80 = $6.80 → savings = $3,200,000 = 32%
math.answer: At least $2,000,000 (20%) in annual savings using single-vendor discount alone; up to $3,200,000 (32%) if volume and single-vendor discounts compound.

brainstorming.prompt: Besides steering wheels, what other car components might GM be able to consolidate across its 10 car lines to generate similar cost savings?

recommendation: Consolidate GM's steering wheel types to a single model across all 10 car lines
Source all steering wheels from one vendor to capture the maximum available discount
This will reduce annual steering wheel spend by at least 32% (from $10M to approximately $6.8M), saving ~$3.2M per year
risks: There may be unforeseen engineering requirements that make a single steering wheel unsuitable for a particular car platform
A single-vendor dependency creates supply concentration risk; disruption could halt multiple assembly lines
Consumer perception research should confirm that wheel uniformity does not negatively affect perceived quality or brand differentiation
risks_from_casebook: Verify no peculiar engineering requirements make the single wheel unfit for any car type
Confirm the steering wheel type does not adversely affect car sales
Ensure the vendor has sufficient capacity to produce at least 1,000,000 steering wheels per year and can scale with demand growth
next_steps: Conduct a rapid engineering audit across all 10 platforms to confirm compatibility with a single wheel design
Issue an RFP or negotiate with current supplier for consolidated single-vendor pricing
Extend the analysis to other high-volume components (headlights, tail lights, moon roofs, dashboard components) that may offer similar consolidation savings
